title: The Weaver Who Met a Royal Tiger (ZH)
summary: A timid weaver carrying a bolt of bright red cloth encounters a tiger in the jungle. Birbal explains how wit turns terror into survival.
full_text:
A notoriously timid weaver named Sukhram was carrying a heavy bolt of bright crimson silk through the dense forest of Mathura to deliver it to a merchant. Suddenly, the bushes parted, and a magnificent Bengal tiger stepped onto the path, barely twenty paces ahead, growling with bared fangs!

The poor weaver was paralyzed with mortal terror. He had no weapon, no tree within reach to climb, and running was certain death.

Remembering an old folk saying that wild beasts fear sudden, unnatural behavior more than weapons, the weaver acted on pure instinct.

Sukhram unrolled the twenty-yard bolt of bright red silk with a loud snap, held the crimson fabric high above his head with outstretched arms, making himself look ten feet tall and twenty feet wide!

Then, instead of screaming in fear, the weaver stomped his wooden clogs against the ground and began singing an energetic wedding folk song at the top of his lungs, marching directly TOWARD the tiger!

The tiger had never in its life seen a giant crimson, singing monster stomping toward it! Terrified by the bizarre red apparition and the deafening noise, the great predator turned tail, leaped into the bamboo thicket, and fled into the hills!

When the trembling weaver reached Agra and recounted his adventure, Emperor Akbar was amazed: 'Is it true, Birbal? Can a timid weaver terrify a royal tiger with red silk and a wedding song?'

Birbal laughed with deep admiration:

'Sire, the most formidable weapon in creation is Presence of Mind!

'A tiger understands the smell of fear; had the weaver run, the beast would have snapped his neck in three seconds. But when confronted with an unknown, bold red spectacle that marched forward without fear, the predator's instinct commanded caution.

'Courage is not the absence of fear; it is the presence of wit in the moment of terror.'

Akbar rewarded the clever weaver with fifty gold coins, celebrating the triumph of ingenuity over brute force.
